intro: Girls gather lotus flowers by a river; young men ride past on horses; one girl looks after them with feigned pride. Mahler gives the girls muted strings, the horsemen a march with timpani, tambourine and mandolin, and the last, long look to a fading orchestra. This is the fourth song of one live 1939 Amsterdam performance of the whole cycle.
question: How does an orchestra turn a glance into a march, and then take the march away again?

sections.label: A · G major — the girls on the bank
B · E major — sleeves and perfumes
C · Orchestral march — the horsemen come
D · The horsemen sung, gallop and bolting horse
A′ · Tempo I subito — the girl’s gaze
sections.mNote: first tempo returns, muted strings, gentler orchestra

cues.title: Comodo, dolcissimo
cues.text: Von der Schönheit (“Of Beauty”) is marked Comodo. Dolcissimo — comfortable, very sweet. Trilling flutes, a horn and muted violins open in G major, with no other brass, harps or percussion yet. Only in the first, fourth and sixth songs does the whole orchestra play, and this is the fourth.
cues.evidence: The first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; IMSLP #20582, printed p. 61) gives the marking and the opening scoring; the Mahler Foundation orchestration and introduction pages state that only songs 1, 4 and 6 use the full orchestra. The recording opens near −31 dB and reaches about −18 dB by 0:05.

cues.title: Girls with lotus flowers
cues.text: The alto sings “Junge Mädchen pflücken Blumen, pflücken Lotosblumen an dem Uferrande” — young girls picking lotus flowers at the river’s edge — over soft woodwinds, harp and muted strings. The metre keeps changing between bars of two and three beats, so the tune sways instead of marching.
cues.evidence: The score (printed pp. 61–62) shows the alto entering with the girls’ text over winds, harp and strings with mutes, and bar lengths alternating between 2/4 and 3/4. The report’s key estimates read G major with correlations up to 0.83 from 0:20; the alto’s entry itself is not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A lotus song, filtered twice
cues.text: The poem descends from Li Bai’s “Lotus-Collecting Song”, set at Ruoye brook in Zhejiang. It reached Mahler through the Marquis d’Hervey de Saint-Denys’s French version and Hans Heilmann’s German, then Bethge’s German paraphrase. Li Bai’s original is eight lines; Bethge and Mahler expand it.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Schönheit page (http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Schonheit.htm) prints Li Bai’s poem, Hervey de Saint-Denys’s “Sur les bords du Jo-yeh” and Bethge’s text, and locates Ruoye brook; Edwin K. C. Li, JRMA 150/2 (2025), fn 3 lists “Cai lian qu” as the generally agreed source; Wikipedia (Das Lied von der Erde, Text) names Heilmann (1905) and Hervey de Saint-Denys (1862).

cues.title: Down a third to E major
cues.text: Around 1:18 the music slips from G major into E major, four sharps, after a ritardando on “wider”, the last word of “spiegelt sie im blanken Wasser wider” (mirrors them in the bright water). The marking is a tempo (ruhiger), calmer, and the violins take their mutes off.
cues.evidence: The local key estimate moves from G major (0:55–1:10, correlation 0.70–0.87) to E minor at 1:15 (0.91), then E major from 1:25 to 1:40; boundaries at 1:18 (0.30) and 1:32 (0.38). The score (printed p. 63) shows rit., a tempo (ruhiger), four sharps and Dämpfer ab.

cues.title: A solo violin and a breeze
cues.text: A solo violin rises above the strings as the alto sings of the wind that lifts the girls’ sleeves and carries the scent of their perfumes through the air. Listen for the solo violin’s long lines and the harp underneath.
cues.evidence: The score (printed p. 64) scores a solo violin (Solo-Vl.) over the lines about the Zephyr; the report shows a louder stretch of about −10 dB with onsets at 5–7 per second from 1:25 to 1:50. The exact entry of the solo violin is not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The singer stops at “Luft”
cues.text: With the word “Luft” (air) the alto falls silent for about a minute and three-quarters. Allmählich belebend — gradually quickening — begins: muted horns, trumpet and trombones, a harp glissando. The boys on horseback arrive in the orchestra before the singer mentions them.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 1:50 (0.46) and 1:54 (0.52) with a level dip to −18 dB at 1:55 and the brightest windows of the first half at 2:10 (about 2,260 Hz). The score (printed p. 65, rehearsal figure 7) has “Luft.” as the alto’s last word before Allmählich belebend; the voice returns at figure 10.

cues.title: Mahler edits the poem
cues.text: Later the alto will sing “Hei! Wie flattern im Taumel seine Mähnen, dampfen heiß die Nüstern!” — how his mane flies, how hot the nostrils steam. Those lines are absent from Bethge’s text as printed beside Mahler’s. Mahler also changes the girl’s pride from “Lüge” (lie) to “Verstellung” (pretence).
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Schönheit page, laying Bethge’s version beside “Text of Das Lied von der Erde (Mahler’s alteration)”; Stephen E. Hefling for UE notes that Mahler retouched Bethge’s poems for his own expressive purposes: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Marschmäßig: the horsemen
cues.text: At Più mosso subito (Marschmäßig) the music becomes a march: timpani with wooden sticks, bass drum, tambourine, mandolin and brass, with two harps. Just before it, around 2:20, the harps sweep a glissando marked “C dur”. A boys’ parade replaces the girls’ idyll.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 2:22 (0.45) with C major estimated at 2:20–2:40 (correlation up to 0.88); onsets rise to 6.4 per second at 2:45–2:50 and the level climbs from −12 dB to about −6.6 dB by 2:55. The score (printed pp. 67–68) marks the harp glissando “C dur” and Più mosso subito (Marschmäßig) with the percussion named.

cues.title: The loudest stretch
cues.text: The march peaks around 3:05–3:20, the loudest windows of the whole song. Trumpets, trombones, horns and percussion carry it; keys flicker through C minor and C major. Notice how much louder this is than the song’s sweet opening.
cues.evidence: The five loudest 5-second windows are 3:15, 3:10, 6:05, 3:05 and 2:55; local key estimates read C minor at 3:00–3:10 and C major at 3:15–3:30. The brass, trombone and percussion parts are read from the score (printed pp. 68–69). The 6:05 window is discussed in the closing cue.

cues.title: p subito: the alto returns
cues.text: Around 3:35 the level drops by about thirteen decibels in one step. The march gives way to Noch etwas flotter (a little brisker) and the alto returns: “O sieh, was tummeln sich für schöne Knaben dort an dem Uferrand” — O see what handsome boys romp there on the bank.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −10.1 dB at 3:30 to −23.1 dB at 3:35 and recovers to −14.8 dB at 3:40, with the key estimate moving to G minor (0.65–0.81). The score (printed p. 70, rehearsal figure 10) has the alto re-entering p subito with Noch etwas flotter.

cues.title: The singer: Kerstin Thorborg
cues.text: Kerstin Thorborg, born in Sweden in 1896, was engaged for Berlin by Bruno Walter, who became her mentor; in 1936 she sang this work under him in Vienna, a live performance that was recorded. By 1939 she had made her home in the United States, singing at the Metropolitan Opera.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, Kerstin Thorborg: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerstin_Thorborg (Walter and the Städtische Oper Berlin; 1936 Vienna Das Lied recording; move to the United States in 1938; Metropolitan Opera until her retirement in 1950); Mahler Foundation history page lists the Walter–Thorborg–Kullman Vienna recording of 1936.

cues.title: Allegro: the gallop
cues.text: After “trabt das jungfrische Volk einher” — the fresh young folk trot along — the alto stops again and the orchestra breaks into Allegro. Flutes play flutter-tongue (Flatterzunge), trombones and tuba play loudly and the strings ride driving triplets. The level climbs towards one of the song’s loud stretches.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −20.6 dB at 4:05 to −7.4 dB at 4:20 with onsets of 5.8–7.6 per second at 4:15–4:30. The score (printed pp. 71–74) has “trabt das jungfrische Volk einher!”, Allegro at rehearsal figure 12, Flatterzunge in the flutes and the bass tuba on the trombone staff.

cues.title: The horse bolts, then stillness
cues.text: “Das Roß des einen wiehert fröhlich auf, und scheut und saust dahin” — one horse neighs, shies and dashes away; hooves crush the fallen blossoms. Then, at Tempo I subito around 4:45, muted violins return, the level falls and the song’s first sweetness is back.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 4:34 (0.44), 4:38 (0.39), 4:44 (0.37) and 4:50 (0.34); level falls to −25 dB at 4:45 and the key estimate returns to G major from 4:50. The score (printed pp. 75–77) has the horse’s words with springing bows (spring. Bogen), then Tempo I subito (Andante) with muted violins marked p espress.

cues.title: The long look, quietly
cues.text: From about 5:22 the texture thins: the report detects only one or two attacks a second, in G major. The alto’s last lines: the fairest girl sends long looks of yearning after him, her pride is pretence, and in her dark glance the heart’s agitation still vibrates. The score’s last marking is Ganz ruhig, quite calm.
cues.evidence: Onset density falls from 5.0 per second at 5:15 to 1.4 at 5:25 and 1.0 at 5:30, with G major estimated with correlation 0.75–0.84 from 5:25 to 5:40. The text and the marking Ganz ruhig are in the score (printed pp. 78–79); the times of the individual lines and of Ganz ruhig itself are not claimed.

cues.title: A conductor who stayed with Mahler
cues.text: Carl Schuricht, born in Danzig in 1880, had heard Mahler conduct his Sixth Symphony in 1906 and led Wiesbaden’s first Mahler festival, including this work, in 1921. Germany banned Mahler from 1933 to 1945; Schuricht went on conducting him abroad, as here in Amsterdam.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, Carl Schuricht: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Schuricht (hearing the Sixth Symphony’s premiere in 1906; the April 1921 Wiesbaden Mahler festival with Das Lied von der Erde, citing Signale für die musikalische Welt; the ban of 1933–45; the 5 October 1939 performance in Amsterdam).

cues.title: Fragments fade
cues.text: In the closing bars the main theme breaks into small fragments and the score dies to a ppp chord. The level trace shows a rise around 6:05–6:10 that is louder than the quiet ending would suggest; this page does not explain it. By 6:20 the level is about 28 dB lower.
cues.evidence: Level is −15.3 dB at 6:00, −5.9 dB at 6:05, −9.6 dB at 6:10, −19.9 dB at 6:15 and −33.4 dB at 6:20, with the strongest boundary at 6:20 (1.00) and a boundary at 6:06 (0.85); brightness is about 1,000 Hz at 6:05–6:10 and 2,300–2,500 Hz at 6:20–6:25. The cause of the 6:05–6:10 rise is not identified from the report. Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note describes the theme breaking into small fragments as the vision fades; the score (printed p. 80) ends pp to ppp with harp and string harmonics.

transitions.title: A ritardando drops G major to E major
transitions.how: The first stanza ends with the sun mirrored in the water. A ritardando on “wider” (mirrors them) stops the flow, and a tempo (ruhiger) restarts it with four sharps in the signature: E major, a minor third below the G-major home key. The violins take their mutes off and a solo violin soon leads, so the change is one of key and colour, not of theme.
transitions.evidence: Local key estimates move from G major (0:55–1:10) to E minor at 1:15 (0.91) and E major at 1:25–1:40, with boundaries at 1:18 and 1:32. The ritardando, signature change, mutes and solo violin are read from printed pp. 63–64 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: The voice stops and the horsemen arrive
transitions.how: The alto’s last word of the second stanza, “Luft”, is also her last for nearly two minutes. Allmählich belebend (gradually quickening) then builds the horsemen out of the orchestra alone: muted horns, trumpet and trombones, harp glissandi and a growing string line. A harp sweep marked “C dur” opens the way to Più mosso subito (Marschmäßig): a march with timpani, bass drum, tambourine and mandolin, where the singer’s sweet tune is gone.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 1:50 (0.46), 1:54 (0.52) and 2:22 (0.45); level and onset density climb to their loudest windows at 3:05–3:20. The text ending, harp glissandi, brass mutes and percussion are read from printed pp. 65–68 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: The march collapses to p subito
transitions.how: The march ends not with a cadence but with a drop in weight: piano subito. At Noch etwas flotter the alto returns with “O sieh, was tummeln sich” over woodwinds, horn, timpani played with wooden sticks and strings. The march’s energy is kept, but the horsemen are now seen from the bank, and the voice, not the brass, tells us they are there.
transitions.evidence: Level falls from −10.1 dB at 3:30 to −23.1 dB at 3:35 and is −14.8 dB at 3:40, with the key estimate moving to G minor. The score (printed p. 70, rehearsal figure 10) has the p subito, Noch etwas flotter, timpani with Holzschlägel and the alto’s re-entry.

transitions.title: Tempo I subito after the gallop
transitions.how: The horse’s rush is written at ever faster paces (Immer fließend, then Immer noch drängender), with the text “Hei! Wie flattern im Taumel seine Mähnen, dampfen heiß die Nüstern!”. Then comes Tempo I subito (Andante): the first speed at once, muted violins marked p espress., a solo violin and harp, and the sun-on-the-water words of the opening (“Goldne Sonne webt um die Gestalten”) return. The excitement disappears in one bar.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 4:34, 4:38, 4:44 and 4:50; level drops to −25 dB at 4:45 and the key estimate returns to G major. The ever-faster markings, the horse’s words, Tempo I subito (Andante), mutes and returning sun text are read from printed pp. 75–77 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Ganz ruhig: the texture thins
transitions.how: The reprised Tempo I settles. The lines about the girl’s long looks and pretended pride come over a sparser, softer orchestra, and the score’s last marking, Ganz ruhig (quite calm), sets the final sung line, “schwingt klagend noch die Erregung ihres Herzens nach” (her heart’s agitation still vibrates). The orchestra then carries on alone in fragments of the opening melody.
transitions.evidence: Onset density falls from 5.0 per second at 5:15 to 1.4 at 5:25 and 1.0 at 5:30, with G major correlation 0.75–0.84; the marking, the thinner scoring and the final lines are read from printed pp. 78–80 of the 1912 full score; the exact bar of Ganz ruhig is not timed.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, IV. Von der Schönheit, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: IMSLP #20582; printed pp. 61–80. Entry times are proportioned between audio anchors at 1:18, 1:50, 2:22, 3:35, 4:45 and 5:25 and are approximate. The mandolin, which has no place in the display vocabulary, is not drawn. Which edition the 1939 orchestra used is not documented.

timeline.note: Trilling flutes, a horn and muted violins open the song.
The alto enters over soft woodwinds, harp and muted strings.
Ruhiger: piccolo, horn and glockenspiel as the girls gather blossoms.
E major: unmuted violins, woodwinds, harp and glockenspiel.
A solo violin rises above the strings at the breeze and the perfumes.
The voice ends on “Luft”; muted brass, trombones and a harp glissando begin to quicken.
A C-major harp glissando and brass with open bells open the horsemen’s music.
The march: timpani with wooden sticks, bass drum, tambourine and brass.
Piano subito: the alto returns over thin woodwinds, timpani and strings.
Allegro without voice: flutter-tongued flutes, trombones and tuba, driving strings.
The gallop reaches its loudest scoring, with trumpets bells up and percussion.
The alto returns for the neighing horse, with springing bows in the violins.
Tempo I subito: muted violins, solo violin and harp return with the sun-on-water words.
Ganz ruhig: the alto sings the girl’s looks of longing over a thin orchestra.
The voice has finished; woodwinds and harp carry fragments of the opening theme.
Harp harmonics and low strings leave a final ppp chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
